summary:
Job opens in prose: "There was a man in the land of Uz whose name was Job. And this man was blameless and upright, fearing God and shunning evil" (1:1). He is not an Israelite — the book calls him "the greatest man of all the people of the East" (1:3) — its author and date are unknown, and the setting has a patriarchal flavor: wealth in livestock, the father sacrificing for his family. Twice the scene shifts to heaven, where Satan — Hebrew ha-satan, "the accuser," a title with the definite article, not yet a personal name — challenges Job's piety: "Does Job fear God for nothing?" (1:9). God permits the test. Job loses herds, servants, and all ten children in a single day, then his health, and responds, "The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away. Blessed be the name of the LORD" (1:21). The reader has seen the heavenly scenes; Job never does — the book never tells him why he suffered.

Three friends — Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar — come and sit with him in silence for "seven days and seven nights" (2:13). Then Job curses the day of his birth, and the book turns to poetry: three cycles of exchanges with the friends (chapters 3–27), a poem asking where wisdom is found (28), and Job's closing monologue (29–31). The friends press one argument from three directions: God is just, so suffering is punishment for sin, so Job should repent. Job insists no sin of his accounts for this and demands a hearing from God, along the way declaring, "I know that my Redeemer lives, and in the end He will stand upon the earth" (19:25; the Hebrew here is difficult and translations differ). He finishes with a sworn declaration of innocence: "Here is my signature. Let the Almighty answer me" (31:35). A younger onlooker, Elihu, speaks for six chapters (32–37), angry at Job for justifying himself and at the friends for condemning without refuting him; the book gives no verdict on Elihu — God's closing rebuke names only the three friends.

"Then the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind" (38:1) — with questions rather than explanations: "Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth?" (38:4). The speeches tour creation — the sea, the dawn, "the storehouses of snow", the Pleiades and Orion, the ostrich, the warhorse — and end with two creatures beyond human power, Behemoth and Leviathan (chapters 40–41). Nowhere do they explain Job's suffering or mention the scenes in heaven. Job replies, "My ears had heard of You, but now my eyes have seen You. Therefore I despise myself, and I repent in dust and ashes" (42:5–6).

Prose returns for the ending. God tells Eliphaz, "My wrath is kindled against you and your two friends. For you have not spoken about Me accurately, as My servant Job has" (42:7) — the defenders of God's justice are the ones rebuked, and they are restored only through Job's prayer (42:8–9). The LORD then "doubled his former possessions" (42:10): the herd counts of chapter 1 reappear at exactly twice the size, and Job again has seven sons and three daughters — this time the daughters are named and receive an inheritance alongside their brothers (42:15). He lives another 140 years and dies "old and full of years" (42:17). In the New Testament, James points to him: "You have heard of Job's perseverance and have seen the outcome from the Lord" (James 5:11).
